summary: Defines SNMP management objects for remote monitoring of switched networks, extending the earlier RMON work to cover switches. It is on the standards track as a draft standard.

eli5.summary: Network switches are like busy train stations. This document gives a standard way to ask them how many trains passed and where they went.

questions: how does snmp port copy work
what is rmon for switched networks
subtitle: SNMP objects that let RMON-style probes watch VLANs, priorities and copied ports on switched networks.

tldr.problem: The RMON and RMON 2 standards assume shared media where every station sees the traffic. Switches do not broadcast data, carve networks into VLANs and prioritize packets, and their monitoring features were all proprietary.
tldr.mechanism: The SMON MIB extends the RMON data source idea so VLANs and physical entities can be monitored, adds per-VLAN and per-priority statistics, and defines a standard port copy table for replicating traffic from switch ports to a monitoring port.
tldr.outcome: Switch vendors get one standard SNMP interface for monitoring and port copy, usable from the same management application that does RMON. It is a Draft Standard and no later RFC replaces it in the unit metadata.

today: RFC 2613 is a Draft Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Switches Need Their Own Monitoring MIB
sections.content:
RFC 2613 defines SMON, a set of management objects (a MIB module) that continues the architecture of the RMON MIB by providing RMON analysis for switched networks. Remote monitoring devices, often called monitors or probes, exist for the purpose of managing a network, and an organization may employ one per network segment.

The RFC lists how switches differ from shared media: data is not in general broadcast, monitoring many entry and exit points needs a lot of memory and CPU, switching brings logical segmentation such as Virtual LANs (VLANs), and it brings packet prioritization. The existing RMON and RMON 2 standards do not cover these things, and the monitoring strategies that vendors built were all proprietary.

The objects are an interface between an RMON agent and a management application, not something for humans to manipulate directly.
sections.eli5: Old monitoring tools were built for a big room where everyone hears everything. A switch is more like many private phone lines, so it needs new tools to listen in on them.

sections.title: Data Sources: Ports, VLANs and Entities
sections.content:
The RMON MIB defines data sources that point to interfaces by ifIndex. SMON extends this so other kinds of things can be data sources. The RFC describes three forms.

  • ifIndex.<I>: the traditional form, called port-based when the interface type is not propVirtual(53).
  • smonVlanDataSource.<V>: a packet-based VLAN, where V is an IEEE 802.1Q VLAN ID between 1 and 4094 inclusive.
  • entPhysicalEntry.<N>: a physical entity inside the agent, where N is an entPhysicalIndex from the Entity MIB.

Because an RMON data source must be tied to an interface entry, the agent MUST create an associated ifEntry of type propVirtual(53) for every VLAN or physical-entity data source. The new dataSourceCaps group lets a management station discover which data sources exist and what they can do. VLAN data sources may appear only once the agent detects VLAN usage, and the agent SHOULD create entries as soon as possible.
sections.eli5: Instead of only watching one doorway, you can now also watch a whole neighborhood (a VLAN) or a part of the building itself. Each one gets a pretend doorway so the old tools can still look at it.

sections.title: VLAN and Priority Statistics
sections.content:
The smonVlanStats group holds control and statistics objects for 802.1Q VLANs. It gives a high-level view of total VLAN usage and of relative non-unicast traffic. The per-VLAN table counts packets and octets, with overflow counters and 64-bit high-capacity counters, and also non-unicast packets and octets. How the agent finds the default VLAN for untagged or priority-tagged frames is implementation specific.

The smonPrioStats group gives a distribution based on the 3-bit user_priority field in the VLAN header. The RFC stresses that these tables report the priority as encoded in the packet, not the priority the switch actually gave the frame.

Both groups use control tables for setup and read-only data tables for results, following the RMON control model.
sections.eli5: One counter tells you how many cars used each lane of the road, and another tells you how many were marked as VIP. It only reports the sticker on the car, not whether the guard actually let them skip ahead.

sections.title: Port Copy
sections.content:
Many switch vendors implemented a port copy feature that replicates traffic from one switch port to another so RMON statistics can be gathered. SMON gives it a standard MIB interface, the portCopyConfig group. Three configurations are described: 1:1 (one source to one destination), N:1 (many sources to one destination) and N:M (many sources to many destinations). Agents MAY limit configurations by interface type, speed, duplex mode, destination over-subscription or resources.

Each row has a direction, copyRxOnly(1), copyTxOnly(2) or copyBoth(3), with copyBoth as the default. Port copy can congest the destination, especially when copying from a faster port to a slower one or from several ports to one, so the MIB offers an optional portCopyDestDropEvents count of dropped frames.

Rows are activated one at a time. In modes 2 and 3 that can give unpredictable results across several set requests, so the RFC RECOMMENDS configuring an entire port copy operation in one SetRequest PDU if possible. A VLAN-based data source MAY be a port copy source but MAY NOT be a destination.
sections.eli5: Port copy is like asking a mail clerk to make a photocopy of every letter going through one slot and drop the copy in your box. If your box is smaller than the slot, some copies get lost, so there is a counter for that.

sections.title: How SMON Fits with RMON and Other MIBs
sections.content:
Copied traffic arriving at a destination port can be a data source for any RMON statistics, and RMON host and matrix entries can be aggregated through the extended data source. SMON uses the RMON alarms and events groups without modification, and an SMON device SHOULD implement the RMON 2 usrHistory group if history collection of SMON statistics is wanted.

SMON relies on the Interfaces Group MIB for the propVirtual(53) type. It does not require the Entity MIB, but entity-based data sources do require the entPhysicalTable. Forwarded versus dropped frame counts are out of scope; the Bridge MIB provides objects such as dot1dTpPortInFrames for that. For VLANs and priorities, interoperability comes from referencing the IEEE 802.1 p/Q definitions.
sections.eli5: SMON does not replace the old tools. It plugs into them and borrows the parts that already work, like the alarm bell.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with read-write or read-create access may be sensitive, and allowing SET operations in an unprotected environment can harm network operations. Three object sets may hold sensitive information: smonCapabilities, dataSourceCapsTable and portCopyTable, so even GET access should be controlled.

The RFC says SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment, even on a secure network such as one using IPSec. Implementors are RECOMMENDED to use the SNMPv3 User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575). Configuring the agent so only legitimate principals can read or change the objects is the customer's responsibility.
sections.eli5: These controls can turn on a photocopier for other people's mail, so only trusted people should hold the key.

items.title: Mode 1: 1:1
items.text: One data source copied to one destination.

items.title: Mode 2: N:1
items.text: Many sources copied to one destination.

items.title: Mode 3: N:M
items.text: Many sources copied to many destinations.

items.label: copyRxOnly
items.desc: Copy only traffic received on the source port.

items.label: copyTxOnly
items.desc: Copy only traffic transmitted out the source port.

items.label: copyBoth
items.desc: Copy traffic received or transmitted; the default.
